Bos , Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief KYIV/BUCHAREST/BUDAPEST ( Worthy News ) – A Russian ballistic missile strike near Ukraine’s capital Kyiv killed at least 10 people and wounded nearly 100 others Friday, Ukrainian officials said, as neighboring Romania, a member of the NATO military alliance, announced it had shot down a drone that entered its airspace. President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the attack, saying rescue efforts were continuing. “A rescue operation is currently underway in the Kyiv region following a Russian missile strike,” Zelensky wrote on social media platform Telegram. “We are still establishing exactly what happened and the fate of all those involved.” Be informed without depending on social media — receive Worthy News by email. Acting Kyiv Regional Governor Ruslan Oliinyk said preliminary information indicated that a Russian ballistic missile struck a private training ground where representatives of Ukraine’s defense industry had gathered for an event. Ukraine’s Council of Defense Industry confirmed that representatives of the sector were present but stressed that it had not organized the gathering. RUSSIA HITS DEFENSE GATHERING One participant, Valerii Borovyk, head of a Ukrainian drone company, said the missile struck during a defense exhibition, describing scenes of panic as people rushed for cover while emergency crews treated the wounded amid the wreckage. Ukraine’s Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko said authorities had launched a criminal probe into possible negligence in organizing the event, while separately investigating the Russian missile strike as a suspected war crime. Separately, officials said a Russian airstrike killed five people and injured nine others in the eastern city of Sloviansk, damaging homes, a shop, and the grounds of Latvia’s consulate. The attacks came as Romania, which shares a 650-kilometer (400-mile) border with Ukraine, announced it had shot down a drone for the first time after it violated Romanian airspace. ROMANIA DOWNS DRONE President Nicușor Dan said a Romanian F-16 fighter pilot destroyed the drone at about 11 a.m. local time. “The area was uninhabited, so the pilot was able to shoot without any risk. Teams are now investigating the incident to establish all the details,” Dan told reporters. Romania’s Defense Ministry said two Romanian F-16s and two Italian Eurofighter Typhoon jets stationed in Romania were scrambled after radar detected the drone approaching from the direction of the Black Sea. Debris landed in a wheat field, causing no injuries or property damage. Military officials said the drone appeared to be a Russian-designed Shahed-type unmanned aircraft, though authorities stressed the investigation into its origin was continuing. REGIONAL TENSIONS GROW Romania has reported repeated drone incursions since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but Friday marked the first time its military has shot one down after an airspace violation. Romania is not alone. Other members of the NATO military alliance, including Poland, have also reported Russian drones or missiles violating or briefly entering their airspace during the war, prompting fighter jet scrambles and heightened security along the alliance’s eastern flank. The latest developments underscored growing concerns that the war could increasingly spill beyond Ukraine’s borders, even as Russia and Ukraine continue exchanging long-range missile and drone strikes with no immediate sign of a negotiated end to the armed conflict. Photograph: Zoe Salt/Zoe Salt @Zoe_salt_photography View image in fullscreen Ultrarunner Sophie Woods climbs up a rocky trail on her way to becoming the fastest person ever to run the Via Alpina, a 2,000km network of alpine trails through eight countries in Europe. Photograph: Zoe Salt/Zoe Salt @Zoe_salt_photography New Zealand ‘So much more respect for myself’: NZ ultrarunner Sophie Woods on smashing a 2,000km alpine run record Sophie Woods speaks about the challenges she overcame while completing the notorious Via Alpina across eight European countries Eva Corlett Thu 13 Aug 2026 20.07 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 20.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A couple of weeks into her record-breaking 2,000km run through Europe’s alps, Sophie Woods feared she might die. Woods and her photographer had just scaled a peak in Switzerland, when a severe thunderstorm engulfed them. “The lightning was going off around us ... there was nowhere to shelter in place [and] all the rocks around us were conductive,” Woods tells the Guardian, from her home in Andorra, nearly two weeks after she became the fastest person ever to run the Via Alpina, a 2,000km network of alpine trails through eight countries. “I was slightly concerned that one of us was going to die,” she says. “I ran so fast to get out of that.” ‘Maybe the suffering is the point’: what does it take to run 163km up and down a mountain? Read more Woods set off from Muggia, near Trieste, in Italy on 4 July to run the mountainous Via Alpina trail winding through Italy, Slovenia, Austria, Germany, Liechtenstein, Switzerland, France, and Monaco with an ambitious goal: complete it in record time. It was an Odyssean feat. As well as battling thunderstorms and several heatwaves, Woods faced another unexpected challenge. At one stage, she had been running since 3am through Austria’s mountains, amid unbearable heat. By mid-afternoon she was exhausted, hot and stressed about whether she and her crew had accommodation for the night. Then, a swarm of blood-sucking horse flies descended. View image in fullscreen Sophie Woods set a new fastest known time on the Via Alpina, completing the 2,000km route through mountains in Europe in 28 days, 17 hours and 59 minutes. Photograph: Zoe Salt/Zoe Salt @Zoe_salt_photography “They were biting me, and I was already at my wit’s end,” she says. “I’m screaming at them every time they bite me. All I wanted to do is curl up in the foetal position and cry.” Unable to outrun them, Woods put away her hiking poles and grabbed two handfuls of ferns. “I spent the next hour just whacking myself with these ferns everywhere and I looked completely nuts. It was horrendous.” In the face of extreme conditions, the 42-year-old New Zealander remained a cautious runner and kept focus – sometimes for 20 hours a day. One ankle sprain, or fall, could have scuppered her goal. Each day she consumed about 7,000 calories, and was supported by her husband, George Woods, and photographer Zoe Salt, who fed her, cooled her down and arranged rests and accommodation along the route. By week three, she felt stronger than ever. “My body was just like, ‘OK, this is our life now … we go out and eat mountains for breakfast.’” Map of the Via Alpina: a 2,000km trail through eight countries Map of the Via Alpina: a 2,000km trail through eight countries. Woods ran through the night to reach the finish line in Monaco on 1 August, shuffling into the glitzy city-state exhausted, and grateful she and her team were still in one piece. “You’ve used up everything … so it just was a sense of relief I don’t have to run any more,” she says. The journey had taken her a remarkable 28 days, 17 hours and 59 minutes – smashing the previous record of 35 days and 21 hours set by British runner Jake Catterall, and beating Dutch runner Tessa Caspers’ previous best women’s time of 38 days. The record, Woods says, also belongs to her team: “It’s a pretty massive thing to ask of anyone, and I’m just so grateful to them.” Realisations and inspiration Born and raised in Christchurch, New Zealand, Woods showed little interest in running as child. After moving to the UK, aged 20, she started running to improve her health, initially managing just 15-minute jogs. As her habit grew, she began running 10km races, which soon escalated to marathons. During the week, Woods worked at a hair salon, while her weekends were spent seeking out mountainous trails. After 16 years in London, she bought a camper van with her husband and spent the next seven years travelling Europe’s mountains, before eventually settling in Andorra. View image in fullscreen Sophie Woods tries to catch a nap while completing her 2,000km odyssey. Photograph: Zoe Salt/Zoe Salt @Zoe_salt_photography Woods has competed in dozens of premiere races, including running the Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (a 170km mountain race) six times, the Tor des Géants (an extreme 330km endurance event) and more, over the past decade. But by 2025, her joy in running started to wane. After several years attempting IVF treatment, Woods and her husband had to come to terms with infertility. As a result, each race felt like she was “just going through the motions”. “I was really struggling with the fact … that my life wasn’t going to look different, that I wasn’t going to be changing nappies and doing school runs,” Woods says. From small-town New Zealand to Mont Blanc: how ultrarunner Ruth Croft made history Read more On seeing his wife struggling, George Woods suggested they focus on a new challenge – Woods running the Via Alpina, with him as crew. The endeavour would have a profound effect on her love for the sport and her sense of self. “I had come from a place with the IVF where I was not particularly in love with my body,” Woods says. “But my love and respect for my body, and what she can do for me now, is just so much more. What she allowed me to achieve, in a way that was joyful … I just have so much more respect for myself.” Since completing the trail, Woods has been flooded with messages from girls and women around the world who want to try a 5km run or push themselves further. Her Instagram account has gained more than 55,000 followers in recent weeks. Woods “never thought” she would be in a position to inspire others and the widespread interest in her feat has come as a surprise. “When you’re in the trail-running world, these things seem a lot more normal,” she says. “But it has blown up, and you start to understand that what you’ve just done is not normal at all.” Explore more on these topics New Zealand Running Ultrarunning Marathon running Europe features Share Reuse this content Comments ( … ) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.upi.com/Top_News/World-News/.text: Tate brothers face new charges in Romania over trafficking of minor Sept. 4 (UPI) -- Embattled influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate faced new charges in Romania related to trafficking and sexual acts with a minor, prosecutors said Friday. Andrew, 39, was indicted for the alleged sexual exploitation of a 15-year-old girl that the brothers moved from Britain to Romania. Tristan, 38, was charged with complicity and attempted obstruction of justice. Romania's Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism said in a statement the charges also include money laundering and pornography involving a minor. The brothers are accused of luring a 15-year-old girl from Britain and coercing her into producing pornographic content through physical violence and psychological manipulation. Prosecutors said the brothers used emotional blackmail, threats, physical aggression and constant surveillance to control the victim and make her produce sexual video chats to sell online. They earned more than $1.25 million by selling the child pornography content, prosecutors said. A Romanian lawyer for the brothers, Eugen Constantin Vidineac, denied the allegations. "We will examine every aspect of it with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process," the lawyer told Newsweek . "Our clients continue to reject the allegations against them," he added. "They have the right to the presumption of innocence, the right to properly examine the evidence relied upon against them and the right to mount an effective defense." The new charges come as the brothers sit in a U.S. jail while they fight extradition to Britain, where they were charged in July with rape, human trafficking and child pornography. The Tate brothers, who hold dual British-American citizenship, have twice been charged with sex crimes in each Romania and Britain. They are former kickboxers with millions of followers on social media. A federal judge in Miami is yet to make a ruling on the Britain's request for extradition after the brothers appeared in court on Aug. 27. Update your preferences in Account Settings Close Reporter Sep 5, 2026 3:12 PM UTC Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered a 72-hour pause in strikes on Kyiv starting at midnight on Sept. 6. The temporary pause coincides with a visit from U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. “Putin has ordered that no strikes be carried out against Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight today,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told state media early Saturday. Ukrainian media had previously reported that its army would observe a ceasefire during the visit, though the details had not yet been finalized. "Such information did come from Ukraine,” Peskov confirmed. Witkoff and Kushner touched down in Moscow later that day to meet with Putin and discuss ending the war with Ukraine. They are scheduled to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday. Read More: What It’s Like to Live in Ukraine, 4 Years Since Russia’s Invasion Both men are real estate developers whom Trump has used as envoys in high-level diplomatic talks. Kushner is also the President’s son-in-law and served as a senior adviser during his first term. “They're bringing with them a proposal to end the war,” U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, calling the two “great negotiators.” The U.S. served as a primary mediator between Russia and Ukraine in 2025 and into 2026. The envoys’ arrival represents a potential revival of that role, which largely stalled in February when Washington and Jerusalem launched joint strikes on Iran, killing the country’s leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei , and igniting an ongoing war . Advertisement Following the Kremlin’s announcement, Zelensky wrote on X that he had been in touch with the envoys and was “ready to observe a ceasefire in airstrikes against the cities involved in the negotiation process.” “From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv,” he wrote, adding that Ukraine is ready for “substantive conversation.” Hours earlier, however, Zelensky posted about an overnight wave of Russian attacks that targeted major airports in Kyiv and Boryspil and killed five people at an industrial site elsewhere in Ukraine. According to the Ukrainian air force, Russia launched ballistic missiles and 167 attack drones in the attack. “Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the U.S. side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport,” Zelensky said. Advertisement Trump attempts to revive stalled Ukraine-Russia peace talks Trump has repeatedly stated that ending the Russia-Ukraine war is a major priority of his Administration, but the reality of that aim has proven difficult . In August 2025, the U.S. President met his Russian counterpart in Anchorage, Alaska, to pursue a ceasefire agreement. The talks proved unsuccessful , and Trump left empty-handed . In October 2025, Trump and Putin planned to meet in Budapest in hopes of furthering peace talks. But the summit was canceled just a few days after the summit was announced after Russia indicated that its hard-line stance on the war had not shifted. “It just didn’t feel right to me,” Trump said at the time. “It didn’t feel like we were going to get to the place we have to get. So I canceled it.” Strain between Trump and Zelensky also impeded progress. In February 2025, Oval Office talks collapsed within minutes when the U.S. President accused Zelensky of being “ungrateful” for U.S. aid and refusing to agree to a ceasefire without security assurances. In the 18 months since, however, that tension has largely dissipated, with Trump saying at this year’s NATO summit that the two had “actually developed a good relationship.” Advertisement The revived push for peace talks comes days after CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew to Moscow last week and met with his Russian intelligence counterparts, a trip that Trump later called “semi-routine,” though it had not been announced to the media in advance and little is known about what transpired. Renewed mediation comes as Ukraine continues to launch some of its largest aerial assaults of the war yet, showcasing the nation’s rapid advancement of drone and missile capabilities in recent months. It demonstrated its growing capacity to strike deep inside Russian territory in August, with strikes landing up to 1,500 miles over the shared border—including attacks on warehouses used by the prominent online retailer Wildberries , after Kyiv said its logistics sites are being used to support the Russian military.
